entry.title: 10 Things That Delighted Us Last Week: Long ’90s Jeans and a Dash of Red
entry.summary: Plus the crispy chili shallots Constance Wu buys in bulk.
entry.content:
We write about hundreds of products each week. Here, in our version of the Sunday circular, we’ve plucked some of our recent favorites: expert-recommended essentials, life-changing stuff you didn’t know you needed, newly launched gizmos, and very good deals we uncovered while trawling through the vast online-shopping universe — including the eyedrops celebrities are clued into, cute heels for high arches, and Hyperice’s newest heated Normatec boots.

Following a recent podiatrist visit, contributor Alejandra Gularte discovered she has high arches. “This makes standard shoes a literal pain to walk in because they weren’t built for me. If sneakers were painful, imagine how heels feel,” she says. Finding nice-looking going-out heels that didn’t look as frumpy as most of the orthopedic options available became her mission. Of the nine pairs she tried, these true-to-size slingbacks were among her winners for all-day wear. She easily walked over a mile in them while thrift shopping, followed by dinner and drinks with her co-workers. And at a ranch-style wedding, walking uphill was painless.

Contributor Angela Tafoya just realized that most of the jeans in her closet are cropped above the ankle, and she wanted to find a versatile pair long enough to graze her loafers and sandals. Landing on “’90s straight-leg” as her search term, she spent time in seven pairs. These were among her winners, and are hard to beat at under $50. Their 30.5-inch inseam made them among the longest she tried, too. She spent a Saturday typically reserved for lounge pants wrangling her kids in these without issue. “They’re cut straight through the hip and thigh, then taper, so they look neat without veering into skinny territory. There’s no stretch, but they were still among the comfiest jeans I tested,” she says.

Teeny e-readers took the internet by storm earlier this year, according to writer Jordan McMahon. But as appealing as they sound, their software was often clunky. When McMahon heard that Boox had come out with the Picco, he decided to test it out. It’s featherlight and just a pinch larger than a credit card, with an easy-to-navigate four-inch touchscreen. “Its hardware has the polish of much more expensive devices, its screen — with a little doing — makes text look great, and the custom software gives this tiny e-reader more functionality than its peers,” says McMahon.

Around a year ago, senior writers Liza Corsillo and Michael Zhao tried on a bunch of Quince coats, where they discovered some gems. This time, Corsillo rounded up five Strategist parents with kids age 3 to 11 to test seven Quince kids coats. Corsillo’s son has worn this thin but cozy and breathable fleece the most, and it still looks great after several washes. “He can wear it like a sweatshirt over a long-sleeve tee or base layer. But it also layers really well under puffers and other heavier coats, and it’s super easy to throw in a bag as a backup layer.” She calls it a near-dupe for a Patagonia fleece he practically lived in last school year.

For this week’s “Celebrity Shopping,” writer Kitty Guo caught up with actress Constance Wu about the crispy shallot-garlic-chili topping she uses a jar of per week. “It’s just so yummy. I put it on rice. I put it on fish. I put it on kimchi. I’ve put it on mashed potatoes. I put it on hummus. It’s really good on salads. And sometimes I’ll sprinkle a little on my hand and just eat it by itself,” she says.

Like most New Yorkers, senior writer Lauren Ro wears a lot of dark clothing when it’s cold. “Incorporating red accents — with a sock or a scarf or pants — is an easy way to liven up the look,” she says, which is why she rounded up over 40 red socks, tights, sweaters, hats, and scarves to sprinkle into your closet this season. Among them is this “scrap of cashmere” beloved by updates coordinator Najwa Jamal. Drape it over your shoulders or tie it over your head like a bonnet, as she does.

“We started hearing about Lumify, the $15 drugstore anti-redness eye drops, when they launched in 2018, and the mentions haven’t stopped since,” says contributor Parizaad Khan Sethi. The solution for red eyes, first recommended to us by Catherine Zeta-Jones, has become an indispensable part of camera-ready routines. Before it, artists were smuggling unsafe and unapproved options from Japan and France.

Brand-name Band-Aids are the convention for small scrapes and wounds, but contributor Michael Hession’s kids aren’t fans. It wasn’t until he spotted his daughter’s wrapped arm after a doctor’s appointment that he realized there could be another option. “This type of wrap is flexible and comfy and clings to itself, not to skin. It comes in rolls and must be cut (or torn) to size and paired with gauze to cover a wound,” Hession says. “It takes an extra 30 seconds of work. What you come away with is a bandage that stays put, doesn’t surrender to a light wetting, and doesn’t leave those annoying bits of backing paper in its wake.”

Writer Arielle Avila recently spoke to ten Strategist staffers about how they caffeinate. “I don’t drink coffee, but I’m a prolific tea drinker,” says writer Kitty Guo. Her tea of choice, by Brooklyn-based Dona, was the most-clicked item in the piece. Guo “immediately fell in love with its high-quality, sustainable tea blends” after discovering them at her local Variety coffee. The giftable library contains the entire range of green, white, oolong, black, and herbal teas. She’ll put a tea bag in her Hydro Flask filled with boiling water and sip throughout the day.

Resident fitness recovery expert and writer Brenley Goertzen has been using compression boots for a decade. “There’s really nothing else on the market that can offer the same experience on rest days,” she says. She tested Hyperice’s 2024 Normatec Elites, but preferred the older Normatec 3 Legs. After trying the Elite Heats for a month, Goertzen thinks they’re a “game changer” upgrade, and not only for recovery. “You can choose from five heat levels ranging from 102 to 125 degrees,” she says, “and seven levels of dynamic air compression,” meaning tension and stiffness in her lower legs dissipates in as little as ten minutes.

entry.title: My Friends Call Me Aretha Franklin With My Camp Snap Cameras
entry.summary: I’ve swapped my iPhone camera for screenless still and video options that are are digital, but with an analog feel.
entry.content:
I like to document the people I love and the places I’ve been — a habit I inherited from my aunties, who often pushed us kids together for a photo at every family event. It was annoying when I was a kid but as an adult, I’ve picked up the mantle. Now, one of my favorite activities is sitting at the table with my grandmother and sifting through decades of family photos, asking about the people or the moments that prompted them.

One thing I love about those pictures is how they look — vintage, filmic. This effect isn’t replicable with my phone’s camera, filtered or otherwise. At some point, I started buying and traveling with disposable cameras, but I’m very lazy about getting film developed, so now I have 10 or so cameras in a box on my bookshelf, some with photos as far back as 2022. I’ve also considered investing in a cheap film point-and-shoot camera, but I know it would be a waste of money, because I haven’t developed the film photos I already have.

Then I learned about Camp Snap, a company that makes screenless digital cameras that capture film-like photos and easily connect to your phone with a USB-C cord: an analog look for the digital age. “The pictures you make are a combination of intention and serendipity,” wrote Strategist senior editor Winnie Yang when she tested the company’s first camera last year. “You have to think a little to frame your shot, but because there are no settings to fiddle with (unlike with all my manual cameras), you don’t have to worry about aperture or shutter speed.” And “because you don’t get to see the result until later,” she added, “you don’t bother taking a zillion versions of the same shot to get just the right one.”

In February, when I went on a vacation to Jamaica with my wife, I brought two Camp Snap cameras — the original camera and the CS-8 video camera, which resembles an old-school Super8. We photographed and filmed everything: the wide mouth of the sea, the food, each other. The results from the still camera were thrilling, superbright and saturated, not unlike the postcards you might buy in a gift shop. The video camera also got us lots of attention — our fellow resort-goers were endlessly curious about the hardware we were toting around.

After we got back, I started taking the still camera everywhere — to dinners, birthday parties, backyard cookouts, weddings. I started fielding comparisons to Aretha Franklin, who often carried a camera with her wherever she went. Without fail people would ask me about it, curious about how it performed and wanting to see the pictures it produced. When I brought it to a wedding, the bride asked for the photos after because a friend told her the pictures were “really good.” I sent lots of links and before long people were asking me to take their photos with it. Then the brand sent me the updated Camp Snap 2, which came out in June, and it became something I don’t leave the house without. While I still use my phone camera, for the moments I want to memorialize, I’m pulling out my Camp Snap.

The video camera is equally exciting. It has the lo-fi look of a home video and performs well in both bright and low light. I recently took it to my friend’s birthday party and then compiled the videos into a recap as a gift. The result looked how the night felt — warm and vibey. Everyone looked soft and beautiful, closer to how I experienced it in real life.

entry.title: Is J.Crew’s New ‘Premium’ Cashmere Better Than Its Regular Cashmere?
entry.summary: New to J.Crew’s women’s Cashmere Shop this season are its “premium” and “luxury” weights.
entry.content:
We’ve long recommended J.Crew’s cashmere. Our contributor Diksha Basu has called it “light, almost like muslin, but in a way that seems like magic.” Senior editor Hilary Reid says it can survive multiple dry cleanings with minimal pilling. “A lot of people come to our store just for the cashmere,” an employee told our former writer (and one-time J.Crew sales associate), Chloe Anello. I’ve been a regular J.Crew cashmere shopper for years, too. No matter what cashmere I try — Uniqlo’s, Quince’s, etc. — I always come back to J.Crew’s. So I was intrigued to learn that the brand’s original cashmere has since rebranded to “signature,” and new tiers called “premium” and “luxury” have been added to the women’s Cashmere Shop. Now, J.Crew’s cashmere weights are feather, signature, premium, and luxury — which are a light weight, a “just-right” weight, a medium weight, and a heavy weight, respectively. Plus there’s brushed, which is described as the brand’s “special fuzzy texture.” Unsurprisingly, the new weights cost more: The premium starts at $178 and luxury $278, compared with the signature’s average $148 price tag. Curious to see if there was a real difference in feel, I recently tried cashmere sweaters in every weight J.Crew offers. For reference, I’m about five-two and I’m wearing a medium unless otherwise noted.

There are very few J.Crew featherweight (now shortened to “feather”) styles remaining in stock. Other than the Featherweight Cashmere Cardigan, the rest of the brand’s featherweight cashmere (the Featherweight Cashmere Relaxed Crewneck Sweater, Featherweight Cashmere Ribbed Sweater-Tee, Featherweight Cashmere Boatneck Ribbed Tank Top …) is nearly sold out (and in the sale department). That’s because, as a representative informed me, the fabrication is being phased out for the season. I understand why. You can really only get away with wearing it between Memorial Day and Election Day. (Reid believed the weight to be ideal “in that it’s warm but not too hot for the fall, and in the winter, I’ll layer a T-shirt underneath.”) Anything colder than 64 degrees and you’re going to be rubbing your arms and saying Brr in it. I found it okay for the unseasonably warm days we had in October. But now that daylight saving time is over, I think it’s just a little too light. And I found it to be near spiderweb delicate. I feared what would happen if a thread got caught in anything, and I noticed some pilling the first time I wore it. Again, I was being careful. Getting the size large was the right call, too, as I think the medium would’ve been too small. This way, it’s vaguely Agnès B. Snap Cardigan–y.

I was worried the rebranded name meant something bad had happened to J.Crew’s signature cashmere. (Like when your favorite neighborhood restaurant gets a new owner.) Thankfully, this is the same dependable mall-brand cashmere I know and love. To be fair, it’s thinner than the premium, brushed, or luxury, but not as thin as feather. And the signature’s weight is on par with Quince’s and Uniqlo’s (cheaper) offerings — but J.Crew’s is softer overall, in my experience. It’s maybe not what you’re wearing in January and February, but in November, December, March, and April, it’ll be great. I ordered a Perfect Cashmere Crewneck earlier this year (pre–signature name change), and this Perfect Cashmere Crewneck seems basically identical. I only discovered a bit of slight pilling under the arms of the crewneck after wearing it with my Alex Mill Cambridge Jacket, likely due to friction with the boiled wool. It usually takes over a handful of wears for me to notice pilling on my J.Crew cashmere from years past. But my Dritz comb fixed this right up.

J.Crew’s premium cashmere is a hair thicker than its signature, but the yarn itself feels heartier (and not at all delicate like the featherweight). It’s closer to the “just-right” weight J.Crew promises the signature to be. It keeps me from sweating and asking, “Is it hot in here, or is it just me?” repeatedly. Sometimes, you don’t need to be that warm — not if your prewar radiator has kicked in, at least — and this makes me feel warm but not warm warm. It’s even warmer than C by Bloomingdale’s cashmere (which I’ve previously described as feeling like you’re wrapped like a love letter in an envelope). Wearing this “premium” cashmere is the equivalent of turning the thermostat up to a sensible 71 degrees. I was happy with J.Crew’s signature cashmere, but after trying the premium, it’s all I want to be in for the next few weeks. I’d even be willing to pay full price, which ranges from $178 to $248.

My least-favorite J.Crew cashmere fabrication is brushed. J.Crew used “longer fibers that are specially washed for an extra-fuzzy texture.” It’s like being nosed by a kitten’s whiskers. For someone with sensitive skin, it can be sensory overload. I couldn’t tell whether I was actually itchy or it was just the nature of the fibers. Another inconvenience is that those very fibers come off in little tufts (rather than standard pills). You’re going to want a lint roller on hand. Something else to note: J.Crew puts the brushed in the middle of the premium and the luxury on its cashmere-weight scale, but I’d say it’s between the signature and the premium.

To my great chagrin, I liked J.Crew’s most-expensive cashmere more than I thought I would. I wasn’t entirely sure the price tag — $278 — was warranted until I tried it on. There’s an immediate, noticeable difference between the luxury, signature, and premium cashmeres. This is a heftier, weightier, and chunkier knit. During every teeth-chattering morning in recent weeks, this is what I reached for. Even as someone who tends to run hot, I felt comfortable in it. With it, you’re more than ready for the next cold front — it’s the perfect middle-of-the-winter weight. It’s giving the Guest in Residence cashmere (which I wore an embarrassing amount of times last January) a run for its money. Part of what you’re paying for, too, is the craftsmanship, like wider, ribbed trims and cable detailing. That said, out of a sheer abundance of caution — given the price — I’d prefer getting it dry cleaned rather than trying to hand-wash it myself.

entry.title: Why Is Every Dancer on Instagram Wearing These Urban Outfitters Sweatpants?
entry.summary: I’m now a convert myself.
entry.content:
It started, as so many rabbit holes do: with my Instagram algorithm. Having deduced that I’ve been taking dance classes, it proceeded to serve me a series of Reels from professional dancers, often featuring the recognizable red backdrop of Millennium Dance Complex in L.A. (if you know, you know).

At first, I watched the videos as merely an appreciative eye, admiring the dancers’ quality of movement, their musicality, and their timing. But my shopping writer brain cannot be turned off, and after a while I noticed that a lot of these dancers seemed to be sporting a certain pair of pants. They were usually navy blue or heather gray, trimmed with white contrast piping down the sides, and baggy as all get-out. They also had a small, subtle logo on the left thigh. Determined to track them down, I took a screenshot, zoomed in and squinted. Through the blurry pixels, I made out the words “Iets Frans.”

A Dutch phrase that translates to “something French,” Iets Frans is Urban Outfitters’ in-house athleisure and streetwear label, offering up sporty hoodies, tank tops, and, of course, plenty of sweatpants. The pair in question were the Harri Wide-Leg Jogger Pants, a slouchy, very oversized style that launched in late 2023 — though it wasn’t until the summer of 2024 that “everyone started posting in them,” says Isabelle David, a student at the University of Illinois and president of the school’s dance crew, ImagiNation. Like me, she originally encountered them online. “I love watching dance classes from big choreographers in L.A. and New York,” she said, “and I remember seeing them and thinking, Wow, they look really good when you dance.” 

From there, they spread like wildfire. Dancers made meme videos poking fun at their own propensity for the pants. Urban Outfitters released them in more colors, from forest green to berry red, and sometimes modeled them on breakdancers posed mid-air or upside down. An out-of-the-loop Reddit user posted in r/dance with a screenshot, asking for an ID, and someone commented that “every dancer under the sun owns these” and “it’s a cult at this point.” Mariel Santos, a dancer, nurse, and content creator based in L.A., estimates that out of 100 students, at least 60 percent of them are wearing the Harris. “Every time I go to Urban Outfitters, the sweats are the first thing I see at the entrance,” she says.

The pants even caught the eye of Charlotte Seet Mun, a dancer and content creator based in Singapore, who also first spotted them on TikTok. However, there are no Urban Outfitters in Singapore, so when she visited L.A. this past March, acquiring a pair was at the top of her to-do list. As it turned out, their surging popularity had made them tricky to come by at the time. “My dad drove me all over LA to different Urban Outfitters and they were all sold out. It was really hard to get them,” she told me, though she did eventually track them down — and now owns five pairs.

Loose, oversized clothing has always been the unofficial uniform for dancers, especially for hip-hop and street styles, to help emphasize and accentuate their movements. “In hip-hop, the movements are very big and explosive. If you wear tight-fitting clothes, you won’t look as big on stage,” Seet Mun explains. But what is about these specific pants that made them catch on so intensely within the dance world? David theorizes the specific cut and material are especially suited for high-intensity movement. The 100-percent-cotton fabric “isn’t too thick where it has a very rigid structure,” she says. “It flows, and that’s visually appealing.” Plus the comfort and breathability of a big, baggy pair of pants can’t be beat. “I hate when sweatpants stick to your skin. These give you a lot of breathing room and don’t feel overly heavy,” says Santos. She’s in the studio five to six times a week, and wears them to pretty much every class. “I own eight, nine pairs,” she confesses. “I have almost every single color.”

At $59, the pants are relatively affordable, even if they aren’t cheap. And the fact that they hold up over time (“The quality is really good, and the color doesn’t wear off,” says Seet Mun), and can be worn casually outside of the studio make them well worth the price tag. David wears them straight from her academic classes to her rehearsals, and Santos has styled them with everything from a leather jacket to a bikini top. “I guess I can either, for lack of a better word, swag them up or swag them down,” she told me.

After hearing these testimonials firsthand, I needed to find out what was so special about these pants, what gave them their je ne sais quoi, that somehow imbues a dancer with more: more power, more grace, more confidence. I called in a pair in navy, size XS. They ended up being a few inches too long (I’m 5’3”), but since the pants have an adjustable drawstring at the ankle to cinch the hem, that solved the issue. I wore them to a hip-hop class — which, having grown up training purely in classical ballet, is the genre I struggle with the most. When I glanced at myself in the mirror, I was struck by how much I looked the part: like a cool hip-hop dancer, fluid and assured rather than stiff and clumsy, as I usually feel. All that excess fabric acted almost like a security blanket, blurring and obscuring any awkward movements — and, by extension, the awkwardness I felt executing them.

It wasn’t just the pants, per se. It was the positive feedback loop generated by the pants: I looked cool in the pants, I felt cool in the pants, and thus was empowered to dance bigger, bolder, less self-consciously.

“When you look and feel good, you dance the best,” Santos told me. Sometimes it’s as simple as that.

entry.title: What Connections Editor Wyna Liu Can’t Live Without
entry.summary: “There’s always one person that gets all the bug bites and that’s me.”
entry.content:
If you’re like us, you’ve probably wondered what everyday stuff famous people add to their carts — like mascara or a sleep mask. We asked New York Times Games puzzle editor Wyna Liu — who recently published the book Connections: Find the Common Threads in 100+ Puzzles of Wit and Wordplay — about the dog treat pouch, Muji essential oil, and benchtop lathe she can’t live without.

I have a dog, Polo, and he’s the best boy in the world, but he’s also kind of naughty. He likes to street snack. I’m in Chinatown, so there’s a lot of food on the street he likes to eat. He has become quite indiscriminate with whether or not something is food, in that he’ll find out by putting it in his mouth first, so I started walking him with a treat pouch. It’s good for me to be able to have something to distract him with so that he looks at me instead of trying to go for a piece of wadded-up gum on the sidewalk. So I walk him with this around my waist every day, and it’s really helpful for keeping his attention. It has these hinges, so you can open it and it’ll stay open. I’ll throw my phone in there too. It’s handy that you can just reach in and grab some treats. The only thing is, you have to be careful to not lean over too far while the pouch is open because then all the treats will fall out on the sidewalk. But Polo loves when it’s a jackpot for him, so maybe it’s not a bug, it’s a feature.

This is meant for you to put in a diffuser, but I don’t have one of those. I just smelled the sample in the store and I was like, I love the way this smells. I keep the bottle by my desk and when I’m feeling stressed, I open it and I smell it. It looks weird, so I try to do it off-camera. I find it extremely calming but also invigorating, like a pick-me-up.

I’m sort of late to the scents game. My mom put the fear of a house-fire in my heart when I was a kid, so we never had candles or incense or anything. It took me a really long time to be like, I can burn a candle, and it’ll smell good. I started using this oil before I discovered that I could also light a candle.

I do hot yoga, but I also just sweat a ton. I’m always sliding around on my mat. I’ve tried a bunch of grippy mats, and this is the only mat that has really been slip-proof for me. It’s quite heavy and cushy, so it’s good if you have a space to leave it somewhere. Lululemon does make a thinner mat that’s easier to carry if you’re traveling to and from a studio. But I love this mat. I’ve been using it for many years, and it works really well.

It looks like one of those old iPods without a screen, and it has one button on it and a little disc. If you get a bugbite, you put the tip of the disc on it and push the button, and it heats up. It gets really hot and it stings for a couple seconds, but then it stops itching. I have no idea how it works, but I love it. If I’m in the park or at a barbecue or something outdoors, and people are getting bitten, I’m like, You’ve got to try this thing. Sometimes people are too scared, which I understand. You have to be brave.

I get bitten a lot. There’s always one person that gets all the bugbites, and that’s me. I don’t know if it’s your blood type, your body temperature, or what. I can be outside for five minutes and I’m already welting up. So this thing has really been amazing for me. I’m less scared of bugbites now.

I’m a Pleats Please evangelist. I feel like these clothes changed my life. They’re so beautiful and easy to care for because they’re machine washable and impossible to wrinkle. The cardigan is something I carry with me every day. It’s practical and beautiful. I can crumple it up, roll it up, and throw it in my bag. Usually it’s my tote bag, but sometimes it’s a smaller purse and it still fits in there. If I’m wearing something casual and I put it on top, it instantly makes me look and feel nicer. It’s one of my favorite pieces, and I wear it every day.

I’m so moved by the thoughtfulness and spirit of innovation that Issey Miyake has had over the years. Like the weaving technologies aren’t just aesthetic, even though they’re so geometric and sculptural. But it also reduces waste, because you can cut the material without it fraying. The pleats particularly landed with me because the sizing is just length. My mom and I are totally different sizes, so we can’t normally share clothes, but Pleats Please is the first time we’re able to. That brings so much joy to me.

I have two pairs of parallel pliers. One of them is urethane-lined, so they’re non-marring. The other is steel jaw. I love these because they’re perfect for holding things securely and evenly. I’ve used them a lot while working with wire. They’re really good for bending it at certain angles because you’re not holding the pliers by one point. You get a really good grip and you can manipulate the material a lot more securely. And they’re fun to use — the mechanism is really satisfying. I didn’t know such a thing existed before, and when I discovered them, I was like, Oh my god, this is exactly what I needed for this certain application.

I was using the pliers to make these little Tensegrity objects. K&S Metals makes these precision rods and tubes that nest in one another, and if you get the right sizes, you can slide the tube into the rod. I use Loctite Retaining Compound to secure it and then you can add the chains. That’s when I discovered that parallel pliers helped me the most to make those bends in the rods. I also use the pliers for jewelry-making. I used them to make my ring, which is another thing that I wear every day. It’s one of my favorite things that I’ve made.

I basically only watch horror movies, which is a little weird. It started years ago when I was working with this material, these white plastic pellets. When you heat them up they turn clear, and then you can mold them into whatever shape you want. I was working on making a deer head, and I was using a heat gun to soften it. A heat gun is essentially a more concentrated hair dryer, so it’s pretty loud. I couldn’t listen to music or watch a movie, because I couldn’t really hear anything. So I started putting horror movies on in the background because you can kind of follow it and enjoy it without needing to know exactly what’s going on. But then I started watching them in earnest.

I love horror as a genre. When you watch a serious drama, you feel all this sadness and suffering, and it feels so emotionally hard. Whereas with a horror movie, it’s gratuitous, but there’s a weird catharsis and comfort and safety where you’re just here for the fun and you know it’s not real. I find that really delightful. I have other subscriptions, but I love Shudder because it’s all horror. They have some really cool movies that I wouldn’t have found otherwise.

I love my lathe. In fact, I have a mug that says “I love my lathe” on it. I first used one when I was in my grad program, which was like a creative technology program at NYU. I discovered that I wasn’t much of a technologist, but I spent all my time in the fabrication shop. I got myself this Sherline lathe after graduating. It was my gift to myself. That was in 2014, so it’s been over 10 years, and it’s held up great. It’s really sturdy and powerful.

You put a piece of metal in the chuck, and a motor will spin it around. Then you can use a cutting tool to make these concentric shapes. There’s something really beautiful and mesmerizing about cutting material on a lathe. It requires focus, but it’s also very beautiful and meditative to see that material spin and change. It’s also very puzzle-y to figure out how to set things up and execute processes in the right order. And in addition to making stuff, you can also make your own tools that you can then use to make more stuff. I find that process so empowering and cool.

I started working at the Times in 2020 as a crossword editor, which is a role that I still have. In 2021, the Times acquired Wordle, and there was a pivot toward developing new games in-house. They started hosting “game jam” events where members of the Games team could come and pitch new ideas and features. Connections was pitched and developed by some of my colleagues, and when they wanted to release it as a 60-day public beta, they needed an editor to write the boards for that test. I was the only editor who didn’t have a game at the time, so they asked if I wanted to try writing them. That’s how I got involved with Connections.

For the book, it was interesting to think about how the experience of solving on paper would be different from solving digitally. It’s really fun to write in a book and doodle and mark up the categories with little glyphs and symbols. The book is a combination of my favorite boards from the archives, and a bunch of new boards in a print-only format. There’s a couple foldouts. There’s some tips and tricks and a little bit of background on how the game is made. There’s a jumbo Connections that’s eight categories, and there’s a meta puzzle where if you solve the eight categories, the first letter of the first word in each category spells something. There are some annotations in the back about certain boards I liked over the years. There’s a “make your own Connections” page at the end that you can tear out and give to someone to solve. It was fun to have a bigger canvas and to think about puzzles specifically for print. And the designers and everyone who worked on it created a really beautiful object. I’m really proud of it.

entry.title: Everyone in My Friend Group Owns the MarshMellow Comforter
entry.summary: It’s delightfully soft and squishy and doesn’t make you overheat.
entry.content:
At least five people in my circle own Mellow’s comforter, and I swear the list keeps growing. Even so, I was hesitant at first to try the MarshMellow from the direct-to-consumer brand, which just launched in 2025, because of its intense social-media marketing. The targeted ads have pictures and videos showing off the ridiculously bouncy and plush volume, which almost seemed too good to be true. When we moved back to our Pittsburgh suburb this fall, though, I finally caved and swapped our Cozy Earth down-alternative comforter with lightweight filling for the Mellow. My fiancé and I have been so happy with our purchase that we already bought a second one for our guest room.

Compared to comforters with a feathery loft, the Mellow one is soft in a mushy, squishy way. It has Oeko-Tex-certified microfiber (polyester) fill, and the fabric shell is 95 percent polyester and 5 percent spandex. While the fill is synthetic, it’s hypoallergenic and naturally resistant to dust mites and has a plump, squeezy, marshmallowy texture that’s very similar to Squishmallows, the popular stuffed toys. The shell has a supersoft, malleable feel that leans smooth and stretchy like a pair of leggings.

Right out of the box, the Mellow comforter looked more dense than other duvets we’ve tried. It almost reminded me of a weighted blanket but is actually mid-weight once it’s been fluffed up and spread out. It feels like you’re wrapped in a cloud, exactly as advertised, but is still breathable for hot sleepers like my fiancé, who keeps our bedroom at 65 degrees every night. Even I — someone who occasionally has hot sweats despite normally feeling cold before bed (I have hyperthyroidism) — have never overheated or needed to kick off this comforter at 3 a.m. We’ve used it through an extremely warm fall in Western Pennsylvania and plan to continue with it on our bed throughout the winter, so it really is fit for all seasons.

I opted to use a duvet cover with the Mellow comforter — which has handy corner loops for just this purpose — as an insert since we have two slobbery dogs. I change out our duvet cover regularly, but I haven’t tried cleaning the comforter yet, though it is machine-washable. (My friend who has washed it at home says parts come out sopping wet, making it impossible to dry since the care instructions say that air-drying it flat is preferred.) The brand recommends using a large-capacity commercial laundry washer, especially for the king size. While this is a hassle, it’s not atypical for a big comforter.

While the plush microfiber fill gives it a pillowy texture, I don’t think it can replace a down comforter. The two options offer entirely different sensory experiences: The Mellow isn’t lumpier by any means, but it’s not as weightless and airy as a comforter filled with goose down. That hasn’t stopped it from becoming my favorite down-alternative pick for anyone who wants a marshmallowlike bedscape year-round. As I write this, more friends have added it to their cart just in time for the holidays.

entry.title: I Got Michelle Obama’s Tiny Timex
entry.summary: Timex’s Cavatina Mini is truly petite.
entry.content:
I started wearing an Apple Watch in 2022 when it came with a subscription to Future, an app-based fitness program that pairs you with a real personal trainer. My husband had already been wearing one for years, but I was resistant to something so bulky and ugly. Soon, though, I couldn’t imagine my life without one. I could monitor my workouts but also keep an eye on emails and messages without being tethered to my phone. I stopped my Future workouts but kept the watch.

Then I began to hate how beholden I was to it. It freed me of my phone but its constant pings and buzzes started to control me. I wasn’t picking up my phone as much, but I was glancing at my wrist every couple of minutes and that felt wrong, too. I also hated how constricting the silicone strap was. Plus, I could never wear a cute analog watch because the Apple Watch had trained me to become so dependent on it.

I finally swapped out my Apple Watch for the new, slimmer Oura Ring 5 a few months ago because I still wanted some biometric-tracking capabilities but in a less obtrusive form. I could now wear a regular watch, and the only one that appealed to me was a tiny Timex that we first spotted on Michelle Obama.

Timex launched the Cavatina in 1959 as its first watch exclusively made for women and recently updated its design to be even smaller than the original watch faces. Obama’s watch is the Cavatina Mini, which has a 17-mm. case — sized down from the 19-mm. Cavatina — and a brushed stainless-steel expansion band. (Strategist deputy editor Simone Kitchens tested this one.) The newest version of the Cavatini Mini comes with a leather strap, and that’s the one I called in.

It’s somehow even tinier than I imagined, but I love it more for that reason. I put it on and it literally feels like nothing. The black crocodile-grain leather strap is so narrow — not much thicker than a standard hair tie — that the adjustment holes basically take up its entire width. It doesn’t get in the way of typing on my laptop or get caught in my sleeve the way the Apple Watch did. The whole thing is delightfully retro (oval face, ’60s-script Timex logo) and understated. If I were a person who accessorized, it would be so easy to create a stack of bracelets just like Obama did with her silver baubles.

The leather watch also comes in a gold-tone case with brown strap, and, soon, in a gold-tone case with deep-red strap (available for preorder). I am also intrigued by the more classic Cavatina, which has a longer oval shape and is two mm. bigger, Roman numerals, and all-caps Timex logo. Still tiny and so wearable.

Bella Druckman, who covers Gen-Z shopping habits for the Strategist, says that this year the gadgets Gen Z-ers used were “all about curating vibes.” Judner Aura, who goes by UrAvgConsumer on YouTube, says people are becoming more interested in creating. “Cameras and microphones are really big right now,” he says. “The low barrier to entry of social media has people inspired and driven to give it a shot.” Technology journalist Joanna Stern, who writes the New Things newsletter, spent much of this year thinking about home robots (that includes robot vacuums). And, of course, the PS5 is on everyone’s list again thanks to the imminent release of Grand Theft Auto VI.

I’ve rounded up all the tech items your loved ones are most likely to ask for this holiday season, and the ones that are most likely to sell out so you can be sure to grab one. It’s worth noting that due to the RAM and storage shortages, tech items such as consoles and laptops can be in short supply and will be quite pricey this year. They’ll still make great gifts, but Aura suggests enhancing what they already have as an alternative. A good accessory goes a long way, after all.

All the perks of a modern MP3 player — including access to music-streaming apps — with hi-fi internals that make it sound better than their phone.

While many have been surprised by the return of wired earbuds, Stern wasn’t. “I’ve been using corded headphones on my computer for forever,” she says. “I just hate using Bluetooth on my computer.” These from Bose have gotten so popular that the company is having a hard time keeping them in stock.

Aura says that for those who are looking to boost the quality of their videos, an external microphone is the first step. This one from DJI is light enough to clip on their collar and has a charging case for up to 48 hours of total recording.

The latest version of JBL’s lava-lamp-like speaker features a light-up handle and a bedside lamp mode that turns this speaker into a lifestyle gadget that’ll do more than just keep the party going. But it’s great for that, too.

With this phone-size e-reader in their pocket, they’ll have no reason to not catch up on their to-be-read list. And since it runs Android, they can even install their favorite news or audiobook apps.

If they need something with a bigger screen, the aluminum version of Amazon’s latest Kindle is about as fancy as an e-reader gets.

Finally, a nice MacBook without the Apple tax.

Just in time for GTA VI. 

Nintendo’s latest console may have debuted last year, but it’s still quite popular, especially with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake that just came out.

A case that’ll ensure they always have enough juice to finish the level.

Or a more comfortable grip that’ll keep their Switch charged for hours and hours.

You don’t need to get them a full-blown console to up their gaming experience, though. This fun accessory turns their smartphone into a portable console, with consolelike controls on both sides. And since it supports Bluetooth, they can pair it with their laptop or console for wireless gaming, too.

“If I’m trying to get some quick shots on the go, this is the camera I use,” Aura says. It’s compact enough to keep in their pocket, ready to capture the moment in a pinch.

With this instant camera, every shot gets printed right away — no printer necessary.

Strategist writer Diksha Basu bought two for her kids.

Apple’s first smart display will play nice with all their other Apple gadgets and can do everything from show step-by-step recipes to managing all their home’s smart lights. And it has a great-sounding speaker, too.

Druckman says that this smart alarm clock — one of our favorites — is popular with teens thanks to its mellow design. “It’s beautiful, and a lot of teens are motivated by that,” she says. She does note, however, that it may not be suitable for college students, as she’s heard it doesn’t always play nice with college campus Wi-Fi.

“If I had a tiny kitchen with only enough space for one smart display,” Stern says, “it would have to be the Skylight. There’s even a rewards system to help keep the kids on track.

Aura just released a smaller version of its e-ink digital picture frame that makes photos look like matte prints. Images on it are truly gorgeous, and they’ll appreciate being kept in the loop with every family moment they may have missed.

Stern is also a big fan of the Matic robot vacuum. “It’s an amazing vacuum and has made incredible leaps this year in software alone,” she says. It’s true: It’s my favorite vacuum too. The keys on Clicks’s latest gizmo are so clicky, they’ll never want to go back to touch typing.

Spare their hands the pain of smartphone pinkie with this luxe phone grip that doubles as a stand.

This portable charger breaks into two parts, so they can always help out a friend while keeping a little juice for themselves.

Help them up their stationery game with a printer that will let them create stickers on the fly.

It’s a Strategist classic for a reason: They won’t find an easier way to listen to in-flight movies with their favorite pair of headphones or earbuds.

entry.title: The 11 Very Best Air Purifiers
entry.summary: For fending off allergens, smoke, and lingering cooking smells.
entry.content:
Whether you’re seeking relief from seasonal allergies, occasional wildfire smoke, or just regular old pollution, an air purifier is a relatively affordable way to make sure the air in your home is as clean as it can be no matter what’s happening in the world outside.

At its core, an air purifier is just a fan that blows air through a filter. In fact, if you’re truly in a pinch, taping five HVAC filters to a box fan (to create what’s known as a “Corsi–Rosenthal box”) does a pretty fine job, as long as you don’t mind the noise. That’s why the most important considerations when shopping for an air purifier have more to do with day-to-day usability than pure performance. However, attributes like the pitch and tone of the fan noise, efficacy of the automatic air-quality sensors, the ease of cleaning prefilters, and how it looks in a home environment are difficult to gauge from a spec sheet. So after researching all the top-rated options available, I tested ten top-rated air purifiers and referred to previous experience with other models to find the best ones.

Updated on November 12, 2026 
The new Coway Airmega Mighty2 is our new top pick for best air purifier overall, and the original Mighty is now our pick for pet smells. I’ve also added the Windmill Air Purifier Max as a pick for people willing to pay for modernist design. The Blueair 2-in-1 Pro is our new pick for humidifying air purifiers. All other picks have been updated with the latest stock and pricing.

HEPA stands for “high efficiency particulate air,” and a HEPA filter, according to the Environmental Protection Agency, “can theoretically remove at least 99.97 percent of dust, pollen, mold, bacteria, and any airborne particles with a size of 0.3 microns (µm).” For physics reasons that aren’t worth getting into here, 0.3µm-wide particles are the most difficult to capture. So HEPA filters are actually even more effective at removing smaller particles (like viruses) and bigger ones (like pollen). “True HEPA,” “medical grade,” “H13,” and “H14” are commonly marketed terms for purifiers that have obtained independent certification for their HEPA compliance, whereas “HEPA-type” is a more misleading term meant to convey certification without having achieved it (and any model labeled as such should probably be avoided).

Clean Air Delivery Rate (CADR) is a performance standard for air purifiers developed by the Association of Home Appliance Manufacturers (AHAM) that consists of three separate tests focusing on dust, pollen, and tobacco smoke and is denominated in cubic feet per minute (CFM). These standardized tests are performed on new machines using new filters by independent labs, which means you can accurately compare ratings across certified makes and models. It’s also a requirement for any machine seeking the EPA’s Energy Star certification, and Energy Star maintains a searchable database containing CADR metrics alongside energy consumption for every certified unit across all brands.

When it comes to mitigating wildfire smoke, AHAM recommends a unit that has a Smoke CADR equal to the size of the room in square feet, which ensures that all the air in the room will pass through the filter at least 4.8 times in a given hour while the machine is running on high. For example, a 300-square-foot living room with a standard-height (eight-foot) ceiling needs an air purifier with a Smoke CADR score of 300. Because CADR is measured on the highest and loudest fan setting, it makes sense to get a unit with more power than necessary so it can still effectively clean the air while running on quieter settings.

Some brands decline to certify, citing the cost of doing so or complaints that the test de-emphasizes attributes they believe are more important than filtration speed. This feels like a cop-out. Toyota may emphasize the Prius’s fuel economy in its marketing, but that doesn’t mean they should withhold the performance figures entirely.

A machine with a built-in air sensor can keep the machine running efficiently on low when the air is already clean, only speeding things up when circumstances demand more. This saves power, keeps noise down, and extends the usable life of the filter and means you never have to worry about fiddling with the settings. While this can’t be determined on a spec sheet, some sensors are more sensitive than others and some brands will tune their auto modes to ramp up fan speeds more aggressively than others. I burned incense to test this behavior on various machines.

Some air purifiers require filter changes twice a year. Others only require annual replacement. A select few claim to last up to five years. This means that two filters that look similar and share the same sticker price may vary in actual cost by up to 1,000 percent, so it’s important to consider filter lifespan when comparing options.

“To filter both particles and gases such as volatile organic compounds (VOCs), many air purifiers contain two filters: a HEPA filter for particles and another for gases,” said Jenna Agins, assistant director of Energy and Sustainability at NYU Langone. This second filter is made from an adsorbent material, commonly activated carbon, which odor-causing VOCs stick to like iron filings to a magnet. Many filters include carbon as either a stand-alone layer or as an integrated part of the main filter. But it’s rarely enough to be an effective long-term solution. If VOC exposure is an ongoing concern, Agins recommends reducing it at the source, for example, by using only low- or no-VOC paints on interior surfaces.

A washable prefilter can trap larger air pollutants like dust and hair before they have a chance to clog up a purifier’s main HEPA filter. Some of these are made from fabric and can be thrown in with the weekly laundry; others are mesh-based inserts meant to be rinsed and/or vacuumed periodically.

HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: 240 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 1-year | Carbon filter: integrated | Washable prefilter: Yes

The Airmega Mighty2 preserves almost everything I appreciate about the original Airmega Mighty (our top pick for nearly a decade and still my pick for pet smells) while making significant improvements. It’s noticeably quieter at every fan setting and a lot more energy-efficient. It has a child lock for the control panel (that also works for pets) and a more accurate laser-based particulate sensor that distinguishes between different-sized particles while providing a live-updating Air Quality Index readout on its built-in display (in addition to the color-changing LED indicator). It also has a light sensor that automatically activates sleep-mode (turning off all displays and indicator lights) once the room lights are off for more than a minute. I used to stare at the blue glow of the older Coway’s status indicator as I drifted off, too tired to get up and do anything about it, but no more!

I’ll confess that I never cared for the original Mighty’s bulbous, chiclet styling, so the new Mighty2’s crisp edges are a welcome sight. But it’s not just for looks; the redesigned vents also help make the machine quieter. It’s virtually silent on low and noticeably quieter on high. And unlike the original Mighty, the Mighty2 never rattles or vibrates while ramping up to its highest fan speeds. On its highest setting, the Mighty2’s more efficient motor saves 18 watts compared to its predecessor (comparable to a USB-C phone charger), which should offset its higher upfront cost within a few years.

The Mighty2’s simplified filter stack is easy to clean and change. The mesh prefilter can now be slid out from the side for cleaning without taking off the front panel. A “PRE” indicator light turns on to alert you when it’s time to do this. The main filter ($70) contains both HEPA and activated carbon pellet filtration and only needs to be replaced annually. The only downside to this more integrated design is that you can’t easily replace the carbon layer with a pet- or pollen-specific filter without also swapping out the HEPA.

The Mighty2’s CADR smoke score of 240 makes it suitable for most bedrooms and smaller, apartment-sized living rooms. Its front-facing air intake vent lets you place it right up against a wall without hurting performance. (Air purifiers with cylindrical filters have higher CADR scores, but those scores are only accurate when the machine is placed far away from any walls or furniture that could impede airflow from any direction.)

HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: 143 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 1-year | Carbon filter: integrated | Washable prefilter: Yes

If you’re only planning to use the air purifier in a small room (less than 150 square feet), the Mighty2 Mini is a good option. A bigger purifier will always be more efficient and quieter (and more versatile should you ever need to move it), but $100 in upfront savings is a significant chunk of change.

True HEPA: No | CADR Smoke: 113 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 1 year | Carbon filter: Yes | Washable prefilter: No

If you must spend less than $100 on an air purifier, the Levoit Core 300-P is one of the most popular, highly rated items I’ve ever encountered on Amazon, with a 4.7-star rating averaged across over 100,000 reviews as of this writing. It is quite solidly constructed, features a responsive touch-control panel, and offers thoughtful features missing from other sub-$100 air purifiers, such as a child lock to prevent interference from kids and pets alike. And it’s pretty quiet compared to other units in its size range, even if it’s whinier than larger units. Its lack of auto mode and washable prefilter are acceptable trade-offs at this price, but I would personally recommend spending the extra $40 to get the more powerful Blue 511i Max in order to have those features if you can afford it.

One thing to note: Levoit stopped advertising the Core 300-P (and a few other units) as being HEPA-certified after a competitor filed a complaint to the BBB. This would give me pause if it was a new unit from an unproven brand. However, since the Levoit’s performance has been validated over the years by independent lab testing (as part of its Energy Star certification), professional reviewers, and many more user reviewers — as well as my own testing — I remain confident in its air-cleaning capabilities.

HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: 410 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 6-9 months | Carbon filter: Integrated | Washable prefilter: Yes

The Blueair Blue Pure 211i Max is about the size of a 50L kitchen trash can, and its CADR Smoke score of 410 CFM means it can quickly clean the air of rooms as large as 615 square feet on its own. This sounds like overkill for smaller homes, but headroom is nice to have on most days — because it allows the machine to run more quietly on its medium or low settings — and it’s critical in case of sudden environmental shocks (such as a nearby wildfire) when greater cleaning power is a necessity.

The Blue Pure 211i Max’s auto mode can access all fan settings and responds quickly and aggressively to changes in air quality in almost real time. Unlike most other units, which gradually increase fan speeds, it kicks into high gear at the first sign of pollution and ramps down as it’s mitigated. This makes it particularly well adapted to combined kitchen-living-dining spaces. Progress can be monitored via the numerical PM counter on top (which can be toggled between PM 1, 2.5, and 10), whereas most other units only have color-coded LEDs. While it’s audibly inoffensive when operating at a steady state, changing fan speeds does temporarily emit a whining noise that sounds kind of like a jet engine taking off.

I appreciate that the Blueair’s washable cloth prefilter wraps around the outside of the unit so you can see clearly when it’s time to launder or vacuum it. (It also comes in several colors if you get bored of gray.) The primary filter costs $70 to replace every six to nine months and consists of a HEPA filter with a layer of activated charcoal for neutralizing odors and other VOCs. For $15 more, there’s also a Smokeblock version that doubles the amount of activated charcoal, and for $20 more, there’s an Allergyblock version that carries additional allergen-specific certifications. All three are available at a 15 percent discount with free shipping if you sign up for a recurring subscription through BlueAir’s website.

It’s also noteworthy that the Blueair app is genuinely useful, and I say this as an appliance-app skeptic. In addition to tracking your home’s air quality over time, it allows you to schedule various modes to run at different times of the day (e.g., sleep mode at night and auto during the day). You can even set the machine to turn off while you’re away and turn on automatically as you approach home (although this requires sharing location data). This can help extend the filter’s lifespan, which the app calculates based on actual usage data.

HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: 450 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: Up to 1 year | Carbon filter: Integrated | Washable prefilter: Yes

Blueair’s Blue Signature is one of the most powerful, quiet, and efficient models available, yet doesn’t sacrifice good design to get there. While the Scandinavian aesthetic may not suit every style of decor, I appreciate that the Blue Signature’s machine-washable cloth prefilter (which slips on and off like a tube top) can be swapped out for a variety of colors, and that its flat top allows it to double as a side table or plant stand. (There’s even the option to add a chrome plinth or wooden table legs, unavailable at the time of my review.) Other new features include a larger, motion-activated display that provides a live-updating estimate of how long it’ll take to clean your home’s air and a wraparound filter design with two additional layers of odor-reducing material. The only catch is the price, which is $100 more than the already powerful and quiet 211i Max.

Whether the Signature is worth the extra cost depends on how well it fits in your home and whether you’ll use all its new features. At 15.5 inches wide, the Signature is difficult to tuck discreetly into a corner, but if you plan to leave it in the open and use it as a side table, that extra width becomes additional usable surface area. I’ve been using it in my kitchen (in place of a 211i Max) and am finding that the additional layers of odor reduction make a difference in dispatching cooking smells that used to linger well beyond dinnertime. (I am curious to see if this is still the case after several months of consistent use.) Other features like “AirSense,” which turns the fan on high for ten to 25 minutes twice a day to refresh the air, are nice to have but only adjustable in the app. The app also lets you monitor the filter’s lifespan, which Blueair claims is up to twice as long as that of their other models. However, at $100 apiece, replacements are also $30 more expensive.

True HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: 286 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 6 months | Carbon filter: Yes | Washable prefilter: Yes

If you want an air purifier that matches your modernist decor and are willing to pay a premium, the Windmill Air Purifier Max offers great performance in a pretty package reminiscent of a fancy planter. It’s even available with a bamboo exterior. It has a front-facing air intake and can sit flush against any wall or piece of furniture. With a smoke CADR score of 286, the Windmill offers better performance than the similarly sized Coway Airmega Mighty2, and it’s comparably quiet. But at $400, with a twice-yearly filter replacement regimen at $79 per set, it costs a lot more. If they happen to be on sale for around the same price, the Windmill’s lifetime warranty (which only applies if you sign up for the filter subscription) gives it a slight edge.

True HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: 153 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 6-9 months | Carbon filter: Yes | Washable prefilter: Yes

The Blue 511i Max has most of the same features as the 211i Max, but is smaller and less powerful and uses a small color-coded LED to indicate air quality instead of a numerical display. This makes it ideal for a bedroom where space is limited and you don’t want to deal with having to activate sleep mode to get rid of any bright lights. Otherwise, it has the same responsive auto mode, washable prefilter, quiet operation, and app support as the bigger unit. Its CADR of 151 can handle most bedrooms with capacity to spare in times of need.

HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: 233 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 1-year (HEPA filter), 6 months (secondary) | Carbon filter: separate | Washable prefilter: Yes

The Coway AP-1512HH may not be the quietest, prettiest, or most powerful air purifier. But its CADR smoke score of 233 is exceptionally high for its compact size. It’s also decent in all other regards: It has an inoffensive design and it’s almost always in stock (which is important for something you might need to pick up in an emergency), and because its intake is on the front and the output vent is on top, it can be placed right up against a wall — unlike many of the columnar designs. This Coway is also one of the few popular air purifiers available with a separate secondary filter. This is helpful because adsorbent materials for trapping odors or other VOCs have a shorter service life than particulate-trapping HEPA filters. Separating these functions means more maintenance, but it also allows you to freely replace the secondary filter anytime you sense it’s starting to fade. This is especially useful if you’re using it to mitigate persistent odors, such as pet smells.

I’ve been using the AP-1512HH with a pet-specific pink filter (formulated to adsorb ammonia and hydrogen sulfide) in the room that houses my two cats’ three litter boxes. It quickly became noticeably less smelly compared to how it was with the all-in-one filter that was previously in there. This may be partly due to the aggressively tuned auto mode, which kicks into the highest fan setting within seconds of me scooping any of the three boxes. The AP-1512HH’s fan noise is a tiny bit whinier than that of our other picks and can be irksome in a living area, but I appreciate it in this context. There’s also a washable mesh prefilter for capturing dust and other larger particles.

Besides the pink filter for pets and the normal charcoal filter for odors, Coway offers a green filter for allergens and a thicker black one for intense smoke, all of which can be found in pairs at this listing for $65, packaged with a single HEPA replacement. (Cheaper imitations abound on Amazon, but using these may void your warranty.) It would be nice if these secondary filters were available separately, but that’s not currently the case.

The Coway’s auto mode responded quickly to burning incense and can access even its highest fan speeds to aggressively clean as needed. This means you can leave it in auto with the child lock activated (which is just as helpful for keeping curious cats from messing with the settings) and trust that it’s keeping your home’s air as clean as possible. Progress is indicated by a status LED that glows blue to indicate clean air, green to indicate some particulates, yellow for a lot, and red if you’re searing a steak without a range hood. While I preferred the more informative, real-time numerical displays found on some other units, it’s enough to assure you that it’s working as intended. There’s no Wi-Fi-connected app to keep track of air-quality levels over time or filter usage over time, but I didn’t miss it.

This Dyson unit is expensive up front, but its five-year filter lifespan and quiet operation make it a great pick for people who just want to put something in their bedrooms, set on auto mode, and not have to think about it. All you need to do is vacuum or dust the exterior every once in a while. The display on the front reports the current air quality and also maintains a color-coded log of recent readings. It’s worth noting that even with the five-year filter lifespan, it doesn’t quite pay for itself compared to a similarly powerful air purifier that requires annual or biannual filter changes, such as the Levoit or the smaller Blueair models. And its CADR of 131 is not suitable for use in larger rooms. The Hushjet’s real value comes from not having to maintain it.

HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: N/A | Auto mode: No | Filter lifespan: 5 years | Carbon filter: Yes | Washable prefilter: No

The AustinAir HealthMate lacks an auto mode and the sleek design of most contemporary machines — it looks like an IBM computer from the 1980s. What it does have is a whopping 15 pounds of activated charcoal and zeolite-absorbent material built into its filter. (For comparison, the entire Blue 211i Max unit weighs just 16.2 pounds.) This means the HealthMate will mitigate smells and other VOCs much more effectively and for much longer than any other machine. However, its $765 price tag is hard to swallow for all but the smelliest situations, even when you account for the filter’s five-year lifespan and pro-rated warranty.

HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: around 240 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 9-12 months | Carbon filter: No | Washable prefilter: No

This Blueair unit is not the most capable humidifier, nor is it the most powerful air purifier, but it manages to be pretty good at both functions while maintaining a relatively svelte profile (it’s only 12.5 inches wide, albeit 24.6 inches tall), so it’s a great choice for homes with limited floor space. It’s not the only humidifying air purifier, but it is the quietest I’ve tested.

The Blueair is designed to be conveniently refilled from the top — you water it like a plant and it finds its way to the removable reservoir at the bottom of the unit, which has a built-in UV light to prevent mold and bacterial growth. I also appreciated that it has an auto-dry mode for the wick that prevents it from getting funky once the 1.3-gallon reservoir is empty. The reservoir has a wide opening, making it easy to clean weekly while in use as a humidifier. Like Blueair’s other purifiers, it uses a single cylindrical HEPA filter that’s easy to replace every 9 months. The humidifying wick lasts about 12 months between replacements. You can track filter and wick lifespan and get reminders of upcoming replacements if you set the machine up with the optional, surprisingly useful Blueair app.

The machine has an LED screen on top that can display relative humidity or the current PM2.5 level in the air. Both of these stats can also be viewed in the app. The touch controls on the top front edge are responsive, and it has a child lock to prevent pets and kids from messing with the settings. I was also disappointed that Blueair doesn’t list the CADR scores for this machine in the specs. (Based on the fact that it is stronger than the previous 2-in-1 and slightly weaker than the 311i, I’m estimating a smoke CADR score of around 240.)

HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: N/A | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 1 year | Carbon filter: Yes + potassium carbonate | Washable prefilter: No

If you have a gas stove and want to lower your home’s NO2 levels without opening the window, most air purifiers won’t be of much help because HEPA filters only trap particles and not gases. Filters that include a separate or integrated activated-carbon layer can be effective for a short period, but they rarely contain enough carbon to last the entire service life of the main filter. Dyson’s De-NOX HEPA filters improve performance and longevity by adding potassium carbonate. This reacts with NO2 and traps the byproducts in the filter, where they remain until it’s replaced (approximately every 12 months). Dyson claims this removes up to 50 percent more NO2 than carbon filtration alone, which aligns with the findings from a 2015 study published in the Journal of Hazardous Materials. New filter and snazzy bronze paint aside, the new De-NOX machines have the same design and pricing as the formaldehyde-eliminating models they’re replacing. Which is to say they’re very nice and very expensive.

The Dyson’s full-color OLED display is easy to read from a distance and responds to changes in air quality in real time. Its fan speed also responded noticeably quicker to any smoke or vapors emitted by my cooking in the adjoining kitchen when compared to other air purifiers. I only wish that the noise was less whiny on its highest fan settings. It’s unusable on speeds eight to ten if you also want to have a conversation in the same room.

Dyson does not believe in the value of CADR for evaluating air-purifier efficacy and therefore does not report these figures. However, Energy Star filings for similar Dyson air purifiers using similar filters indicate a flow rate of around 80 CFM for smoke. This means it is most suitable for use in a smaller bedroom or office.
